recentItems.title: Claire Foy and co-stars in Danny Boyle's 'Ink' arrive at Venice Film Festival
recentItems.description:
(2 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS
Venice, Italy - 2 September 2026
1. Mid of (left-right) Claire Foy, Guy Pearce, Danny Boyle and Jack O'Connell on a boat
2. Various of "Ink" cast and director sailing away
3. Pan of Claire Foy, Guy Pearce, Danny Boyle and Jack O'Connell on a boat arriving
4. Wide, push in on Foy, Pearce, Boyle and O'Connell disembarking
5. Close of Foy
6. Close of O'Connell
7. Push in on O'Connell and Pearce
8. Close of Pearce
9. Mid of Boyle, joined by writer James Graham
10. Wide of cast and crew of "Ink"
11. Pan of cast and crew of "Ink"
12. Pan of Foy leaving
13. Wide of O'Connell signing autographs
STORYLINE:
Claire Foy, Guy Pearce, Jack O'Connell and Danny Boyle sailed into Venice on Wednesday to discuss their new film "Ink," which is in competition and opening the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. 

"Ink" is a film about the rise of media tycoon Rupert Murdoch and “The Sun” editor Larry Lamb.

Directed by “Trainspotting” filmmaker Danny Boyle, “Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s acclaimed play, which dramatizes Murdoch’s 1969 acquisition of the daily newspaper “The Sun.”

Guy Pearce plays Murdoch and Jack O’Connell plays Lamb in the film about how they turned the paper into Britain’s most influential tabloid. Claire Foy also co-stars.

recentItems.title: Gaza: padres palestinos destruyen o esconden cometas por amenaza de represalias israelíes
recentItems.description:
(2 Sep 2026) 
SLUG: GAZA NIÑOS COMETAS SP 
Source: ASSOCIATED PRESS
No additional restrictions beyond those terms outlined in your license agreement.

Producción de: Wafaa Shurafa

Gaza: padres palestinos destruyen o esconden cometas por amenaza de represalias israelíes
 
———————————————————————————————————————
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Jan Yunis, Franja de Gaza - 26 de agosto de 2026
 
Las cometas, globos y drones, antes imágenes habituales en el cielo de Gaza, ahora casi han desaparecido después de que el gobierno israelí amenazara con atacar las zonas desde las que se lanzan hacia Israel. 
 
SONIDO (árabe) Imad Mortaja, desplazado en Jan Yunis: 
“Mis hijos estaban jugando con una cometa cuando oí que empezaban a bombardear y a amenazar a quienes tenían cometas”, dijo este padre de tres hijos. “Destrocé la cometa por la seguridad de mis hijos y de quienes los rodeaban”.
 
SONIDO (árabe) Imad Mortaja, persona desplazada en Jan Yunis: 
“La cometa no les hace daño alguno y, sin embargo, destruyen manzanas residenciales enteras”, dijo.
 
Tras descubrir en un kibutz cercano a la frontera con Gaza, varias cometas que no transportaban armas ni materiales peligrosos, el primer ministro Benjamin Netanyahu y el ministro de Defensa, Israel Katz, amenazaron en un comunicado con intensificar los ataques si Hamás no garantiza que dejen de volar drones, globos y cometas hacia Israel. 
 
Para las familias la pérdida de este sencillo pasatiempo ha sido un duro golpe y estos padres describen una infancia para los niños acorralada por todas partes. 
 
SONIDO (Arabe) Atiya Abu Samhan, desplazado en Jan Yunis: 
“Nuestros hijos, cuyos sueños han sido destrozados lo han perdido todo, sus sueños sencillos, su educación, su infancia, las cosas simples que solían disfrutar”, dijo este desplazado.
 
SOUNDBITE (árabe) Reem Abu Samhan, desplazada del este de Jan Yunis: 
“Si salen, hay bombardeos. Si vuelan una cometa, hay bombardeos. Si van a la escuela, hay bombardeos. Si van a la playa a relajarse, hay bombardeos”, dijo Abu.
 
ANNE MARIE GARCIA, ASSOCIATED PRESS


STORYLINE:

recentItems.title: Syrian exhibition revisits Assad-era prisons through objects left behind by detainees
recentItems.description:
(2 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY: 

ASSOCIATED PRESS  
Damascus, Syria -  31 August 2026
1. Various of exhibition visitors crowding around prison cell and taking pictures

ASSOCIATED PRESS  
Damascus, Syria - 1 September 2026
2. Man looking at writings on a wall at exhibition
3. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Abdul Wahab Yasser, relative of a former prisoner:
“My cousin died in the Kfar Sousse branch, and this wounded me deeply. I came here expecting to see his name on the walls, but I didn’t find his name. I wanted to find any part of him, even if it is writings on the wall.”

ASSOCIATED PRESS  
Damascus, Syria -  31 August 2026
4. Clothes of former prisoners under the Assad regime
5. Close of sign reading (Arabic) "transferred as it was"
6. Various of people taking pictures of clothes 
7. Display showing socks
8. Display showing keys
9. Display showing prosthetic limbs
10. Rusty handcuffs in display case
11. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Walid al-Hussein, General Directorate of Prisons and Correctional Facilities, Syrian Ministry of Interior:
“The pavilion has real things that once belonged to (prisoners) from inside Saydnaya prison and other branches that were run by the fallen (Assad) regime. All the clothes and keys and other things were transferred to this show as they were in the prisons.”
12. Al-Hussein talking to a man by a wall which is displaying pictures, top writing on wall reading (Arabic) "Rehabilitation center and the beginning of hope"
13. Tilt down from a prisoners' food menu to al-Hussein
14. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Walid al-Hussein, from the General Directorate of Prisons and Correctional Facilities, Syrian Ministry of Interior:
“In the near future, we aspire to change this punitive philosophy of killing and torturing detainees in prisons, that was followed by the old regime, into a new system that safeguards the human dignity of the inmate by providing healthcare, good and nourishing food, and a clean environment.”
15. People looking at a picture of Saydnaya prison
16. Woman taking a picture of a photo of her killed relative that she put on a prison door
17. Sign reading (Arabic) "torture devices"
18. People looking at signs and objects of torture devices
19. Woman crying

ASSOCIATED PRESS   
Damascus, Syria - 1 September 2026
20. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Abdul Wahab Yasser, relative of a former prisoner:
“No words can describe the pain that we are living. Those who want to come here must have the ability and will to stomach (such an exhibition). My heart might be too vulnerable for such a place.” 

ASSOCIATED PRESS   
Damascus, Syria -  31 August 2026
21. Sign reading (Arabic) "When Walls Speak", which is the name of the exhibition 
22. Various of people visiting the exhibition
STORYLINE:
The old prison cell is dimly lit and dirty, with thin mattresses scattered across the floor. 

Soiled clothes and personal belongings hang from the ceiling, while scratched names and other writings cover the walls.

Visitors crowd around the exhibition, taking photographs and videos, some staring into the reconstructed cell with vacant looks.

At the Damascus International Fair, Syria's Interior Ministry has created an exhibition called “When Walls Speak,” displaying objects from prisons and security branches that operated under former President Bashar Assad.

The exhibition includes cell doors filled with prisoners' writing, clothing, lost keys, rusty handcuffs and artificial limbs. It also displays items the ministry says were used to torture detainees.























For him, simply walking through the exhibition was devastating.

recentItems.title: Maggie Gyllenhaal says 'systemic problem' is behind lack of women in Venice competition
recentItems.description:
(2 Sep 2026) 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Venice, Italy - 2 September 2026
1. Wide shot Maggie Gyllenhaal arrives at press conference, followed by Alberto Barbera
2. Medium shot press conference with jury panel
3. Wide shot press conference
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Maggie Gyllenhaal, jury president:
(Reporter: "I'd like to know if you think cinema should be political, political, especially now.")
"Might as well get into it. I will speak more to this tonight, but I guess I believe, look, we could say how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency? To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves. Personally, I don't believe that there is any subject or any filmmaker that shouldn't be heard. I think we can challenge ourselves to hear stories about the most corrupt, the most perverse people because it opens up the opportunity to find empathy for those people and even to look at the ways in which we might have a little bad guy inside us, a little perversity inside us a little corruption inside us, fight it as we might."
5. Wide shot press conference
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Maggie Gyllenhaal, jury president:
"I am here open, I am here curious. I think that if movies really are an honest look into other people's experience, that they are fundamentally, unavoidably, political, as well as a lot of other things."
7. Wide shot panel
8. SOUNDBITE (English) Maggie Gyllenhaal, jury president - joking about the lack of women in the competition:
"I guess it's just finally become clear that men make better movies than women do! I will answer you seriously and say that there's a systemic problem, obviously. I do think it's much harder for women to get their films financed. Also, could it be possible that the things that women having had a different experience of being alive in the world want to make movies about are not always deemed high art? Who decides what's good? Who decides what's valuable? I will also say, sitting next to one of the people who makes that decision that I am on a panel here with many, many women and have also on my jury, incredible female filmmakers. But I will also say that that's also a question I have and it's a legitimate one."
9. Wide shot press conference
10. SOUNDBITE (English) Maggie Gyllenhaal, jury president:
"Yes, I do think that there's a systemic complication, confusion, about what is valued. I think it's been such a short time that women have had the opportunity to make films at all and there will be, it will take some time to get used to the fact that I think many women make movies quite differently than men do. I will also say, you know, as I said, I really am walking in with a question as to why there's so few women in the main competition as filmmakers this year, but I think Alberto and Julia asking me to be the head of the main jury competition after the two films in particular that I have made is a very important thing to consider too."
11. Various shots press conference ends
STORYLINE:
Maggie Gyllenhaal, president of the Venice Film Festival’s main jury, used a press conference ahead of the festival's opening on Wednesday to address the lack of women directors in this year’s competition. 

Of the 21 films competing for the Golden Lion, only one is directed by a woman, a disparity Gyllenhaal called evidence of a “systemic problem.”






“I think that if movies really are an honest look into other people's experience, that they are fundamentally unavoidably political," she said.

recentItems.title: Ariana Grande, her fans and the final show
recentItems.description:
(2 Sep 2026) 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
London - 1 September 2026
1. SOUNDBITE (English) Ariana Grande, recording artist:
"This has been one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life and I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely. Thank you from the bottom of my heart. It has been so special. I’ll cherish this experience always. I have the best fans in the entire world and I always have."
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Sasha Tsenova, fan:
(Reporter: "What do you think about her taking a bit of a break now?) 
Tsenova: "It's really annoying."
3. SOUNDBITE (English) L-R: Tilda Ashbee and Tabby Ashbee, fans:
Tabby Ashbee: "I think she's worked hard. She deserves a break."
Tilda Ashbee: "I think also everyone just needs to shush online, just everyone needs to talk to themselves."
Tabby Ashbee: "Keep quiet."
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Jake Farenden and Joe Price, fans:
Price: "Honestly, I don't blame her. With all the public scrutiny on her,  I don't blame her. I think she needs a well-needed break."
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Sasha Tsenova, fan:
(Reporter: "But surely she deserves it.")
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Cheyenne Griego, Milton Beltran
and Adrian Garcia, fans:
Garcia: "She needs it. I think she needs it, she has worked her a** off and has always worked her a** off so it's about time." 
Beltran: "Well deserved."
Garcia: "Well deserved, you know. No explanation to anybody. Ari, go. Go. That's it."
7. SOUNDBITE (English) L-R: Tilda Ashbee and Tabby Ashbee, fans:
"Obviously if I had the same things I would definitely take a break, so she deserves it
8. SOUNDBITE (English) Sasha Tsenova, fan:
Tsenova: "Oh, come on, why is Ariana Grande taking a break? She's so good!"


PRODUCTION BY: HILARY FOX
